findings.evidence: Ordinary ice is less dense than liquid freshwater near its freezing point, so a floating cube displaces its weight in liquid while remaining partly above the surface.
Hydrogen bonding arranges water molecules into an open crystalline lattice during freezing, increasing volume for the same mass.
Liquid freshwater reaches its maximum density near 4 °C rather than becoming steadily denser as it cools all the way to freezing.
Floating depends on relative density; the explanation applies to typical water-based drinks and should not be generalized to every possible liquid.

editorial_angles: Start with density, then explain the molecular reason that ice has lower density.
Distinguish density from mass: a cube can weigh the same after freezing but occupy more volume.
Use buoyancy to explain why most of an ice cube remains underwater.
Clarify the 4 °C maximum-density point for freshwater without suggesting all water behaviour is simple.
Mention exceptions: floating depends on the surrounding liquid's density, not on ice having a universal tendency to float in every fluid.
